newsitem.title: UGANDA: Uganda rejects bid by Swiss firm for coffee unit.
newsitem.headline: Uganda rejects bid by Swiss firm for coffee unit.

text.p: The Ugandan government has rejected a bid by Swiss company Sucafina for 51 percent of Uganda Coffee Marketing Board Limited (CMBL).

"We have rejected Sucafina's offer. We have invited other bids and the only way Sucafina may be considered is if they raise their current bid," said Matthew Rukikaire, minister of state responsible for privatisation.
In September, Sucafina offered to pay $3.3 million for the 51 percent shareholding.
Rukikaire said that bid was too low.

CMBL assets included in the sale were valued at $36.7 million. The company's principal asset is its central processing and storage unit in Bugoolobi. It has export processing capacity of four million 60-kg bags a year.
Ugandan coffee officials said privatisation authorities felt a foreign buyer would have to offer at least two thirds of the $36.7 million.
Privatisation authorities were willing to sell CMBL at a lower rate only to Ugandan investors, they added.
Rukikaire told reporters that Ugandan bidders were the automatic choice in the sale of state companies if their bids were equal to or only slightly below those of foreign companies.
CMBL also owns two storage units at Bugoolobi with a combined capacity of 40,000 tonnes and is equipped with a rail line and truck loading platform, according to bid documents.

As part of its efforts to restructure operations and to take advantage of its large processing capacity, CMBL maintains primary processing facilities in the growing areas of Budde, Kawoko, Kiira and Ndese.

Geneva-based Sucafina was the only bidder for the CMBL stake, submitting its offer two minutes before the deadline on September 26. It sought to buy the 51 percent stake in two tranches, one of $1.8 million and one of $1.5 million.
Rukikaire told reporters that his privatisation unit was examining proposals by a group of Ugandan investors interested in buying the shares in the marketing board.

A senior official in Rukikaire's office said, "As the coffee industry is so essential to the economic well-being of Uganda, it is important that we carefully consider each bidder's business plan and investment commitment prior to reaching any decisions regarding the sale."
CMBL's share of the coffee export business fell to 9.4 percent in 1995, from around 84 percent four years earlier.
Uganda has more than 100 private coffee exporters.
The Uganda Coffee Development Authority (UCDA) has forecast coffee procurement at between 3.6 and 3.8 million 60-kg bags in 1996/97 (Oct/Sept), down from 4.2 million in the previous year.
